job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: David Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in cybersecurity at Westmoor University, and I live at home in Port Alder with my parents and my grandfather. I get up early, help my dad open the hardware store, Silva and Sons, then catch the train to lectures. In the evenings I do capture-the-flag puzzles with a small club and then I eat my mother's dinner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you work in the store much?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Saturdays and holidays, mostly. I like the customers, and I know where every screw is, which my dad finds funnier than I do. My bachelor's in computer science was a pass, with no internship, because I was working in the store through the summers, and I got my security basics from online courses instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, and what I'd expected from the start. I'd tell my friends at the club that it still pays to learn the basics well. At church I'd say nothing, because nobody asks me about computers there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plan is the plan. Finish the master's, then work as a junior security analyst at a bank or a hospital in the region. There's demand, and my parents' savings mean I don't have to take the first job that appears. I use the tools now and then to read logs faster, but they don't do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to about twelve security teams from February, and keep practising on the club's puzzles every week. I'd do a recognised certificate, the one employers ask for, which costs about four hundred. I'd keep helping on Saturdays at the store and make a spreadsheet for Dad's stock, free of charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A plateau is good for a man who likes learning one thing properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cybersecurity?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People attack systems whether AI is hype or not. Every company I know has been hit by something, and the store lost a day to a scam email last spring. I thought, someone should know how to stop this, and I'd like it to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would be most affected if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandfather, believe it or not. He's eighty and keeps cash in a tin and distrusts the bank app. If nothing changes, he's fine. If anything does change, he'd be the first confused, and he'd call me.

say: That's fine, and what I'd **expected** from the start.
I'd tell my friends at the club it still pays to learn the **basics** well.
think: My plan is the plan: a junior **security analyst** job at a bank or hospital.
My parents' savings mean I don't have to take the **first job** that appears.
do: Apply to about twelve **security teams** from February.
Do the **certificate** employers ask for and make a stock spreadsheet for Dad.
feel: **Calm**: a plateau is good for a man who likes learning one thing properly.
S0.quote: Someone should know how to stop this, and I'd like it to be me.
fieldNote: A **settled** young man whose reasons for the field come from a store scam, not from hype.
Mentions his **grandfather** unprompted, which shows how much his family frames his choices.

steps.text: Apply to twelve security teams from February
Do the recognised security certificate for four hundred pounds
Build a stock spreadsheet for Dad's store

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's good and bad, like any new tool, and the important thing is that people keep their work. At the club I'd say attackers will use AI too, so security people get busier. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty good about it. Security work is partly checking and monitoring, which the tools help with, but someone has to decide what matters and talk to frightened people. Attacks get faster with AI, so defenders are needed, even if there are fewer junior jobs. My pass degree worries me a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and do the certificate, then apply to security teams, and I'd learn the main AI security tools properly, as I think employers will ask. I'd offer to run a free security check for three local shops, including ours. It'd give me stories for interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. It feels like the world is catching up to my choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would more AI make your field safer or less safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. The tools find problems faster, and the attackers write better scam emails. I'd say it's an arms race, so my sort of job gets more necessary. I'd feel safer if more small firms paid for a person to look after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at your father's store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's supplier already wants orders by app, and the till software is getting clever about reordering. He'd resist at first and then say yes because it saves him an evening each week. I'd sit with him to set it up and check it's secure.

say: That's good and bad, like any new tool, and people should **keep their work**.
Attackers will use AI too, so security people get **busier**.
think: Someone has to decide what matters and **talk to frightened people**.
Fewer junior jobs exist, and my **pass degree** worries me a little.
do: Finish the **certificate** and learn the main AI security tools properly.
Offer free **security checks** to three local shops, including ours.
feel: Pretty good, as if the world is **catching up** to my choice.
S1.quote: Attacks get faster with AI, so defenders are needed, even if there are fewer junior jobs.
fieldNote: He sees AI as **more work** for defenders, which is why he stays calm even with a pass degree.
Plans free checks for local shops, **giving back** and building stories for interviews at once.

steps.text: Learn the main AI security tools after the certificate
Run free security checks for three local shops
Sit with Dad to set up the till's reorder software securely

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is serious and we shouldn't panic, but we shouldn't joke either. I'd tell friends to look after family first. At church I'd ask for a conversation about helping the people who work in offices, because they'd be hit hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried. In two years the thinking work, even security analysis, could be done by AI, and I'd have just finished the master's. The robots come around 2031, which would catch Dad's store too, in stocking and delivery. I'd feel the ground moving under three generations of my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and look for work that needs people on the ground: security for physical sites, infrastructure, hospitals. I'd keep my savings and help my father decide whether to buy a stock robot or not. I'd also join a union or an association of professionals, if one will have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd say my prayers more, and I'd still lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we've got through bad times before, and we'll do it again, but we need to sit at the table and be honest. My mother would make coffee, my grandfather would say something sharp, and my father would say we'll see. I'd watch them all and try to look calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in cybersecurity?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not in the same way. I'd aim for the security side that deals with people and real equipment, such as locks, cameras and hospital devices. If an AI can do the log reading, I want to be the one in the building when something goes wrong.

say: This is serious, so **don't panic**, but don't joke either.
I'd ask for a church conversation about **office workers** who'd be hit hardest.
think: Even security analysis could be done by AI, and I'd have just **finished my master's**.
The ground would be moving under **three generations** of my family.
do: Look for security work with **physical sites**, like infrastructure and hospitals.
Help Dad decide on a **stock robot** and keep my savings.
feel: Anxious: I'd say my prayers more and still **lie awake**.
S2.quote: If an AI can do the log reading, I want to be the one in the building when something goes wrong.
fieldNote: His family-first reaction shows **traditional** values: three generations at one table.
His plan shifts to **physical** security, the part of his field that robots reach later.

steps.text: Look for physical security jobs at hospitals and infrastructure sites
Help Dad decide whether to buy a stock robot
Keep the savings and cut the training budget to essentials
Join a professional association for security staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time to be calm and a short time to be idle. I'd tell friends to learn, save and look after their families. I'd ask my parish to organise advice evenings for people who might lose office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy. I'd have a first job for two years or so, then the thinking AI arrives, then the robots in 2034. I'd be thirty by 2031, and I'd want a house and a family. My field might be one of the last for people, but I wouldn't bet everything on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a security job and save hard, aiming for a deposit on a small house. I'd learn the main AI tools, since the job will ask. I'd marry my girlfriend Lucia, if she says yes, and talk to Dad about whether the store should add services like security cameras and fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not frightened. It feels like a long winter I can prepare for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with five years that you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be firefighting. With five I can build something. A deposit, a trade skill like installing alarms, and a family I can look after. I'd want to be less dependent on any one employer, so I'd start a small side service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandfather?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to worry, and then I'd explain it with a hammer. A tool is a tool until it starts using you. Then I'd make him a cup of coffee and ask him about the war, since he likes to tell me how people got by.

say: Five years is a long time to be calm and a short time to be **idle**.
I'd ask my parish to run **advice evenings** for people who might lose office jobs.
think: I'd have a first job for **two years** before thinking AI arrives, then the robots in 2034.
I'd be thirty by 2031 and want a **house and family**.
do: Take a security job and save hard for a **deposit** on a small house.
Talk to Dad about adding **alarm fitting** and cameras to the store.
feel: Uneasy, not frightened: a **long winter** I can prepare for.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be firefighting. With five I can build something.
fieldNote: He sets **marriage and a house** inside his plan, so family goals shape his saving.
Considers **alarm fitting** at the store, tying his skill to his father's business.

steps.text: Take a security job and save for a house deposit
Learn the main AI security tools used on the job
Add alarm and camera fitting to the store's services
Propose to my girlfriend Lucia and plan the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a mercy. I'd tell friends to build careful lives, learn what they can and keep their families close. I'd also tell them to vote for whoever takes it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. By 2036 I'd be thirty-four, with ten years in security, a family and a house, and the store might be a security and hardware shop. Robots come around 2039, and that's far enough to see coming and adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work as a security analyst, move to team lead in five years, and keep a side service for local businesses. I'd get married, buy a house and save for my children's education. I'd learn the AI tools as they become standard, one at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some gratitude. A decade is time to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd work, save and marry. In the next five I'd grow the side service and move up. I'd leave bigger bets, like buying the shop building, until the world is clear, around 2033 or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a church or club where older people teach younger people, because the community stays strong when people know each other. I'd also like the town to run a free evening class for adults who want to learn the new tools without feeling stupid.

say: Ten years is a **mercy**, so build careful lives and keep families close.
I'd tell friends to **vote** for whoever takes it seriously.
think: By 2036 I'd have ten years in security, a family and a **house**.
The store might become a **security and hardware** shop.
do: Become **team lead** in five years and keep a side service for local businesses.
Marry, buy a house and save for my children's **education**.
feel: Calm, with some **gratitude**: a decade is time to do things properly.
S4.quote: I'd want a church or club where older people teach younger people, because the community stays strong when people know each other.
fieldNote: His long horizon gives a **life plan** with marriage, house, children and a side service.
Wants **community classes** where adults can learn without feeling stupid, a gentle, practical idea.

steps.text: Work as a security analyst and aim for team lead in five years
Marry Lucia and buy a house
Grow a side security service for local shops
Back a town evening class for adults learning new tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd be finishing the degree just as it might stop paying, and three generations at one table would feel it. What would help is honest information from the government, retraining that employers have agreed to, and a community that keeps meeting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that the quiet people, the ones who keep a store open and look after their parents, are the ones who'd hold it together. They should be asked.

headlineQuote: The quiet people, the ones who keep a store open and look after their parents, are the ones who'd hold it together.
portrait: David is a **24-year-old** cybersecurity master's student who lives with his parents and grandfather in Port Alder.
He works Saturdays in the family hardware store and uses AI **now and then** for reading logs.
He is traditional and steady: **family, faith** and community shape every plan he makes.
His mood is calm in four worlds and **anxious** in the two-year one, which would hit three generations.
His fallback is **physical** security work, a house, a side service and the family store.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because he'd finish his degree just as it might stop paying.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **information**, retraining that employers agree to, and a community that keeps meeting.
